description: "How NCodeGroup .NET code registers, resolves and scopes services in Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection: lifetimes and captured state, options-validation cycles, TryAdd and TryAddEnumerable, marker-builder prerequisites, start-up ordering, and choosing the right shape for an extension point."
applyTo: "**/*.cs, **/*.csproj, **/Program.cs"

# Dependency injection

<!-- Generated by `npm run train` from the sources each rule cites. To change a rule for good, change its source or say so in training/feedback.md; the next training run regenerates this file. -->

- **In production code, keep singletons free of per-request, per-user and per-session state: never memoize a request's result on a singleton (for example `_result ??= await ...`). Keep that state on the request, such as in `HttpContext.Items`, a request context object, or a scoped service that no singleton captures.** The first request's answer leaks to every later request. A client-authentication result memoized on a singleton let later requests reuse it whatever credentials they presented. *Check:* Look for mutable fields, lazy caches or `??=` assignments on singleton-registered types that are filled from request, user or session data. *Note:* Don't report a singleton that holds a concurrent cache of the application's own data, such as its own client tokens, when the keys come from configuration and app-owned credentials and no request or session data goes into it. A singleton that holds the current user is acceptable only in a single-user WebAssembly host. Its registration's remarks must say it is for that host only and name what serves the server and prerendering side, because a server host that runs the client registration for prerendering would share the user across requests. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1381; Identity outcomes of #600</sub>
- **Never capture a scoped service in a singleton. A singleton that dispatches to scoped services creates a new scope for each call with `IServiceScopeFactory` and resolves those services from it.** A captured scoped service outlives its scope, which leaks state and disposed instances across callers. *Check:* Look for singletons that take scoped services in their constructor, or that cache handler instances, instead of resolving them from a scope created per call. <sub>Identity ADR-1047</sub>
- **In background work, create an `AsyncServiceScope` (`CreateAsyncScope`) for each unit of work, such as each job attempt or each tenant group, and resolve scoped services and handlers from it, never from the root provider. If the work needs request-like context, create that context inside the scope and dispose it before the scope.** Background work has no request scope. Each unit needs its own scoped dependencies and tenant context, and async-disposable services have to be disposed correctly. *Check:* Look for hosted services or workers that resolve scoped services from the root `IServiceProvider`, that reuse one scope across attempts, tenants or the whole service lifetime, that use a synchronous `CreateScope`, or that never dispose the context they created. <sub>Identity ADR-1223; Identity ADR-1242; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, never store request or ambient context (`HttpContext`, the request, a `ClaimsPrincipal`, user values, a request-scoped `IServiceProvider`) in a field or property of a long-lived type. Read it where it is used, take it as a parameter, or make the type a live view over `IHttpContextAccessor`.** Captured context goes stale, outlives its request, leaks across requests and makes the type hard to test. *Check:* Look for fields or properties of those types, or values copied from them at construction, on singletons or other long-lived objects. *Note:* Don't report a context value object created for each call and passed to a callee, such as a validation context that carries the `HttpContext`. Before reporting, check whether a factory creates the type per call or per request, or whether it is a registered long-lived service. <sub>Identity convention-audit.instructions.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #600</sub>
- **Don't let an `IValidateOptions<T>` depend, directly or through the services it resolves, on the options type it validates. That covers `IOptions<T>`, `IOptionsMonitor<T>` and `IOptionsSnapshot<T>`, and any component or `IEnumerable<T>` of handlers whose constructors read them. To list registered names or capabilities, read a descriptor-only catalog or plain data that constructs no services.** Reading the options from inside their own validation recurses and deadlocks the host at start-up, and the container can't detect that cycle. *Check:* Trace the constructor dependencies of each `IValidateOptions<T>` and setting-descriptor source. Report an options accessor of the same `T`, or services and handlers it resolves that read that `T`. <sub>Identity ADR-1137; Identity ADR-1145; Identity ADR-1400</sub>
- **Don't resolve a service that only becomes available once a hosted service's start phase has run (for example a keyed key-ring provider loaded by a warm-up) from an eager singleton constructor, an options validator, `ValidateOnStart` or an existence check. Check existence through a registration query or the provider abstraction's `Has…` method, and resolve the service only when a request uses it. Document the ordering constraint in the registration's XML summary, and make early resolution throw an `InvalidOperationException` that names what has not been loaded yet.** Resolving it earlier fails at start-up, and an ordering dependency that isn't documented is hard to diagnose when a later consumer resolves it too early. *Check:* Look for `GetRequiredKeyedService` or a DI factory that returns state filled in by `IHostedService` or `IHostedLifecycleService`, called from constructors of singletons, from validators or from start-up checks. Check also that the constraint is documented and that the failure message says what is missing. <sub>Identity ADR-1479; Identity outcomes of #709</sub>
- **Check whether a named resource exists through the abstraction that resolves it, such as a provider's `Has…` method, not by querying keyed DI (`IServiceProviderIsKeyedService`, `GetKeyedService`) or the underlying store directly.** A host can replace the provider with a source that isn't keyed DI, and a check that bypasses the provider would refuse names the replacement can resolve. *Check:* Look for validation code that queries keyed DI or the store directly when a provider interface is the seam that resolves the resource. <sub>Identity ADR-1439</sub>
- **In production code, keep the constructor of a provider that validators or capability readers may resolve (such as a remote key-management provider) free of I/O, option reads and client construction, and say so in the type's XML documentation.** Validation can end up resolving such providers, so a constructor that reads options, builds an SDK client or calls the network would do that work during plain validation, and could also run into the options-validation cycle. *Check:* Look in provider constructors for `IOptions` access, SDK client construction or network calls, and check that the type's XML documentation states that the constructor does no I/O. <sub>Identity ADR-1474</sub>
- **When start-up work must run before every hosted service's `StartAsync`, implement it in `IHostedLifecycleService.StartingAsync`. When a start-up check needs state that a hosted warm-up loads, make it a hosted service registered after that warm-up, not a startup validator or `ValidateOnStart`.** Every `StartingAsync` runs before any `StartAsync` whatever the registration order, while every startup validator runs before any hosted service starts, and so before the warm-up has loaded anything. *Check:* Look for hosted services inserted at index 0, or ordered by registration only, so that they run first. Also look for `ValidateOnStart` or `IStartupValidator` logic that reads state a hosted service creates, and for gate services that aren't registered after the service they depend on. <sub>Identity ADR-1247; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Make a dependency that enforces isolation or security, such as a tenant-scope accessor taken by a DbContext, a required constructor parameter with no optional, nullable or unscoped fallback.** Isolation has to fail closed: a missing registration must be a start-up failure, never a silent loss of isolation. *Check:* Look for such dependencies declared optional or nullable, or that fall back to an unscoped default when they aren't registered. *Note:* Tests and tooling that construct the type directly pass an explicit unscoped implementation instead of relying on a default. <sub>Identity ADR-1018</sub>
- **In library code, register a default implementation with `TryAdd*` (`TryAddSingleton`, `TryAddScoped`, `TryAddTransient`), never with `Add*`. This covers default adapters for ports, replaceable validators and policies, and pluggable resolvers, so a host that registers its own implementation first replaces the default.** Consumers implement, decorate or replace a capability in one place, and `TryAdd*` lets their earlier registration win. Validation done inline in endpoints can't be replaced and drifts apart. *Check:* Look for `AddSingleton`, `AddScoped` or `AddTransient` of a default service in a library's registration extensions, and for validation or policy logic inlined in endpoints instead of going through a replaceable service. <sub>Identity ADR-1039; Identity ADR-1204; Identity ADR-1205; Identity ADR-1424; Identity ADR-1500; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Register each implementation of an open, multi-implementation service (handlers, event handlers, fan-out command handlers, rules, formatters, blocklists, descriptors, strategies) with `TryAddEnumerable`, or with a helper built on it, and inject the set as `IEnumerable<T>`.** The set is open: packages and consumers add implementations next to the built-ins by registration, and a registration method that hosts call together, or call twice, must not register the same handler twice. *Check:* Look for collection-style services registered with `AddSingleton`, `AddScoped` or `AddTransient`, which duplicate, or with `TryAdd*`, which block additions, and for implementations gathered in a hard-coded list. <sub>Identity ADR-1047; Identity ADR-1051; Identity ADR-1112; Identity ADR-1114; Identity ADR-1144; Identity ADR-1201; Identity ADR-1205; Identity ADR-1206; Identity ADR-1236; Identity ADR-1285; Identity ADR-1390; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Don't use `TryAddEnumerable` for several instances of one implementation type. Give each built-in strategy its own class, and register data instances that share a record type with an instance-aware add that finds and replaces an existing entry by its identifying key, such as a name or tag.** `TryAddEnumerable` keeps one registration per implementation type, so it silently drops the other instances, such as other curves or algorithm specifications. *Check:* Look for `TryAddEnumerable(ServiceDescriptor.Singleton(instance))` where other instances of the same concrete type may be registered. *Note:* Don't ask for `TryAddEnumerable` where instances of one record type are registered on purpose through a documented replace-by-key step. Check the registration's doc comment or decision record before reporting. <sub>Identity ADR-1392; Identity ADR-1402; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #548</sub>
- **Make registration methods give the same registrations in the same order whatever order the host calls them in. When the order of an enumerable registration decides a default (such as the first item being the fallback), have each method finish by sorting the registrations into a canonical order that depends only on which items are registered.** Otherwise the default depends on the host's composition order. Nothing documents that, reordering `Program.cs` changes it without any test failing, and it breaks docs that promise the method can be called before or after the main registration. *Check:* Look for methods that append to a shared enumerable registration where calling them in a different order changes which item is first. Check that tests cover the different call orders. <sub>Identity ADR-1402; Identity outcomes of #548; Identity ADR-1230</sub>
- **A library that decorates a service the host may also register must handle both registration orders. Replace the last non-keyed registration in place, keep its lifetime, and wrap whichever of its instance, factory or implementation type it uses. If none is registered, add the decorated default. Never wrap a registration that is already decorated.** Hosts register the service before or after the library call, `TryAdd` keeps an earlier registration, and wrapping twice would apply the decoration twice. *Check:* Look for decorator registrations that only use `Add` or `TryAdd`, that change the lifetime, that ignore `ImplementationInstance` or `ImplementationFactory`, or that have no guard against wrapping twice. <sub>Identity ADR-1238</sub>
- **Register services with `TryAdd*` unconditionally. Don't guard a registration with `services.Any(...)` and an early return that skips the services registered after it.** If something else registers the guarded service first, the early return silently leaves the dependent services unregistered. *Check:* Look for `Any(...)` checks followed by `return` or a conditional `Add*` in DI extension methods. <sub>Randomness outcomes of #12</sub>
- **A registration method that removes services the host may have registered, for example with `RemoveAll<T>()` or `Replace`, must say in its remarks that it replaces them and why.** A host that registered its own implementation earlier would otherwise lose it without notice. *Check:* Look for `RemoveAll` or `Replace` in `Add*` extension methods with no matching XML remarks. <sub>Identity outcomes of #600</sub>
- **In production code, make a registration that hooks, decorates, replaces or consumes another library's services extend that library's marker builder (`IServiceBuilder<TMarker>`) instead of a bare `IServiceCollection`. Extend the marker of the library whose services it actually resolves and calls, not a lower library's.** The receiver type proves at compile time that the prerequisite library, and everything beneath it, is registered. A bare collection turns a missing prerequisite into a confusing runtime failure. *Check:* Look at the `this` parameter of new `Add*` extensions: is it `IServiceCollection` or the wrong library's marker, when the method uses another library's services? <sub>Identity ADR-1051; Identity ADR-1062; Identity ADR-1069; Identity ADR-1390; Identity ADR-1405; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Take a second prerequisite as a required `IServiceBuilder<TMarker>` parameter, the builder that prerequisite's registration returned, and return the receiver builder. Every registration that others depend on, custom stores and other dependency-inverted seams included, must create and return its own marker builder.** Anyone can `default` an empty marker struct, so only a builder that the prerequisite's registration created proves anything. Dependents can demand that proof only if the prerequisite hands one back, and returning the receiver keeps the chain on the primary library. *Check:* Look for prerequisite parameters typed as a marker struct, as an optional or nullable builder, or as a custom proof type. Also look for methods that return something other than their receiver, and for store or seam registrations that return `void` or the bare collection. <sub>Identity ADR-1051; Identity ADR-1057; Identity ADR-1069</sub>
- **Express registration prerequisites only through builder types. Don't add runtime checks that probe the container for another library or for the feature itself, such as `IsRegistered`, `Any(d => d.ServiceType == …)`, throwing on a missing prerequisite, or an endpoint that returns 501 when its feature isn't registered.** With opt-in packages, being registered is what makes a feature present. Runtime probing moves an avoidable mistake to start-up and depends on order, whereas typed builders turn it into a compile error. *Check:* Look for registration code or endpoints that inspect the service collection or provider for their own registration or for a prerequisite's. <sub>Identity ADR-1057; Identity ADR-1069</sub>
- **In production code, take a bare `IServiceCollection` only for registrations that stand alone: chain roots that create a marker and have no prerequisite, one-service utility helpers, and marker-less cross-cutting infrastructure. Make a helper that several libraries' builders call extend the non-generic `IServiceBuilder`.** Ask whether the registration would work if it were the only thing registered. The non-generic builder still requires the caller to hold some library's builder without tying the helper to one library. *Check:* For each new extension on a bare collection, ask whether it depends on another library's services. For shared helpers, such as message factories or endpoint providers, check that they don't extend a bare collection or one specific library's marker. <sub>Identity ADR-1069; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Define a registration marker as an empty `readonly struct` that implements `IRegistrationMarker<TMarker>`, and declare it in the library's `.Abstractions` package.** The marker's type is the whole signal, so it carries no data to keep in sync, and consumers that reference only the abstractions must be able to name the builder. *Check:* Look for marker types that are classes, that have members, or that are declared in an implementation package. <sub>Identity ADR-1069</sub>
- **In production code, have the package that owns a consumer register that consumer's framework dependencies (routing, `IHttpClientFactory`, authentication, `AddDataProtection()`, `AddMetrics()`, `TimeProvider`) with `TryAdd*` or the framework's idempotent `Add*` call, so composing the package is turnkey. Add `TimeProvider.System` only through `TryAdd`.** A host shouldn't need to know a package's internal prerequisites. Wiring that works only because an unrelated call such as `AddControllers` pulled them in breaks when that call is removed, and `AddSingleton<TimeProvider>` would replace a test clock the host registered. *Check:* Look for packages that resolve such services without registering them, hosts that rely on an unrelated call for side effects, and `AddSingleton<TimeProvider>`. *Note:* Don't suggest moving a package's own infrastructure registration, such as `AddMetrics()`, out to the host. Exceptions: a library that a decision record deliberately limits to DI and hosting abstractions may leave `IMeterFactory` to the host, because every generic and ASP.NET Core host registers it. Also don't ask a registration method to register, require or validate a dependency when some of its callers, such as migration workers or design-time DbContext factories, never resolve the service that needs it and its XML doc says the host supplies the dependency. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1247; Identity outcomes of #529; coordination outcomes of #18; Identity outcomes of #807</sub>
- **In library code, don't register or configure host-wide infrastructure: no `IDistributedCache` or other shared store (`AddDistributedMemoryCache`, `AddStackExchangeRedisCache`), no Kestrel `ConfigureHttpsDefaults` or other last-wins host configuration, and no OpenTelemetry SDK or exporters. Depend on the library's own ports and on `System.Diagnostics`/`System.Diagnostics.Metrics`, and leave the choice of adapter to the host's composition.** A library that registers these decides them for the host and for every other consumer, and `ConfigureHttpsDefaults` keeps only its last action, so it silently replaces the host's TLS settings or is replaced by them. *Check:* Look for these calls, or for OpenTelemetry SDK package references, inside library projects or library registration extensions. <sub>Identity ADR-1164; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1202; Identity ADR-1197</sub>
- **When a library or capability registers an authentication scheme, register it as a named scheme and never override a default scheme the host has set (`DefaultScheme`, `DefaultAuthenticateScheme`, `DefaultChallengeScheme`). Make it the default only when the host has not set one.** Overriding the host's default silently changes how its other endpoints authenticate. *Check:* Look for `AddAuthentication(scheme)`, or for default-scheme assignments made unconditionally, inside library registration code. *Note:* One source says a capability's cookie scheme must never become the default. A later source allows a library's scheme to become the default when the host has set none. Both forbid overriding the host's choice. <sub>Identity ADR-1062; Identity ADR-1292</sub>
- **Model a capability that only some backends or deployments can supply (resolving a login hint, notifying an authentication device, changing a password) as its own seam. Register with `TryAdd*` a default that fails safe by reporting 'unsupported' through its normal result, and let the package that supports the capability replace it whatever order the registration methods run in. An opt-in capability's own registration must not register a default backend or turn the capability on.** A backend that can't support the capability just says so, which keeps the protocol correct and secure until a deployment supplies its own behavior. A required member on a shared interface would force answers most implementations can't give. *Check:* Look for members added to shared backend interfaces that most implementations can't honour, defaults that throw `NotImplementedException`, succeed silently, or approve or resolve users, defaults registered with plain `Add*`, overrides that work only when called before or after the default, and capability registrations that wire a backend by default. <sub>Identity ADR-1062; Identity ADR-1085; Identity ADR-1086; Identity ADR-1230</sub>
- **In production code, choose each behavior's DI shape on purpose. Use a plain `IFoo` service with a default implementation, called directly, for a capability that callers ask for an answer. Use a `TryAddEnumerable` strategy collection for implementations the caller iterates over or selects among. Use an `NCode.Mediator` command or pipeline only for request-pipeline steps that consumers must override or that many contributors mutate, or for cross-cutting wrapping.** Each behavior should take the cheapest shape its requirement allows. Mediator dispatch hides the handler and adds ceremony, while overridable, multi-contributor seams need its priority ordering, post-processing and unified exception handling. *Check:* Look for new command/handler pairs whose only caller sends the command to get a result, for fan-out mediator commands where the caller could loop over `IEnumerable<T>`, and for overridable pipeline steps built as direct services. Also look for handlers that implement ordering or post-processing themselves instead of using `ISupportMediatorPriority` and `ICommandResponsePostProcessor`. <sub>Identity ADR-1001; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Don't select behavior with a `switch` or if-chain over an open vocabulary's names or enum members (PKCE methods, client-authentication methods, response media types, holders of protected values). Register each member's behavior as its own strategy class and dispatch to it by name through a strategy collection or catalog.** A switch that needs a new case for each extension shuts out packages that can't edit it. With strategies, a new value is just a new registration. *Check:* Look for switches, if-chains or hard-coded lists over vocabulary values that pick an implementation, and for inline branches such as `if (response is X && prefersHtml)` where a registered formatter would do. <sub>Identity ADR-1150; Identity ADR-1144; Identity ADR-1285; Identity ADR-1289; Identity ADR-1114; Identity ADR-1407; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Validate a strategy catalog or name-keyed set when it is composed, not when it is first looked up. Its constructor throws `InvalidOperationException` for empty names, duplicate names, input that two strategies both accept, references to unregistered entries, and handlers and descriptors that don't match one to one. Resolve that component in a hosted warm-up service so a mismatch fails at host start, after options validation.** A duplicate or ambiguous name could be handled by either strategy, an unmatched descriptor advertises something nothing handles, and a handler with no descriptor is never advertised. Checking at composition makes a bad registration fail at start-up instead of on the first request. *Check:* Look for catalogs that match strategies or descriptors lazily at request time, that silently pick the first of several matches, or that have no start-up resolution. Also look for removal of an existing correspondence check. <sub>Identity ADR-1145; Identity ADR-1285; Identity ADR-1289; Identity ADR-1389; Identity ADR-1400</sub>
- **In production code, when one mediator handler depends on another's effect, state the order with handler priorities. Never rely on registration order.** Registration order is an invisible, fragile dependency, and mediator handlers run in descending priority order. *Check:* Look for handlers whose correctness assumes they are registered before or after another handler. *Note:* For contributed strategies that may accept the same input, one decision record uses registration order as the host's preference order instead of adding priority numbers, and refuses input that two strategies accept as ambiguous. Don't ask for priorities there. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1389</sub>
- **Reach a host-replaceable behavioral hook (a delegate the host configures at start-up) through the abstraction-level type that declares it, never by injecting `IOptions<T>` of an implementation package's options.** Injecting the implementation's options ties the consumer to that package, and consumers that reference only abstractions can't do it at all. Each surface then implements the hook its own way, and the host's override is honored on some surfaces and ignored on others. *Check:* Look for `IOptions<…Options>` injections used only to read a delegate, and for consumers that reimplement a hook's logic. Check that a new hook is declared on the abstraction type and wired from the options in the implementation. <sub>Identity ADR-1053</sub>
- **In production code, constructor-inject every dependency. Don't `new` up a collaborator or a shared service (such as a cache or lock table) inside a method or constructor. Register it, for example with `TryAddSingleton`, so the container owns and disposes it, and inject it. Keep separate uses of one shared instance apart with keys that include their purpose. Inject `IEnumerable<T>` for a fixed set of singletons.** Private instances can't be substituted in tests or shared with other registrations, their separation holds only by convention, and injecting the shared instance later would silently merge their key spaces. *Check:* Look for `new` of service-like types, especially types also registered in DI, in fields, constructors or methods. *Note:* Test projects may use a private sealed nested stub that one test file needs. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #520; Randomness outcomes of #12</sub>
- **In production code, use service location (`HttpContext.RequestServices`, `GetService`, `GetRequiredService`, `GetServices`) only when a singleton resolves a scoped or open-generic collaborator at the point of use, when a generic type argument picks the service at call time, or in framework glue marked `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]`.** Limiting service location keeps dependencies explicit and lifetimes visible, and the allowed cases stay testable through a real `ServiceProvider`. *Check:* Check each service-locator call against these cases. *Note:* This rule doesn't apply to test projects. <sub>Identity convention-audit.instructions.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Send outbound HTTP through a named `IHttpClientFactory` client, not a private `SocketsHttpHandler` or a raw `new HttpClient`. Create `HttpMessageHandler` instances, including inner handlers that a wrapping handler disposes, inside the `ConfigurePrimaryHttpMessageHandler` or `AddHttpMessageHandler` factory lambda, never outside it and captured.** The factory is the seam a host uses for telemetry, resilience and test-server handlers. It also rotates handler chains and disposes the old ones, so a captured inner handler is already disposed when the next chain uses it, and calls fail with `ObjectDisposedException`. *Check:* Look for `new SocketsHttpHandler`, `new HttpClient` or custom handler-source interfaces in outbound code, and for handler instances that a factory lambda captures from outside. <sub>Identity ADR-1381; Identity outcomes of #465</sub>
- **Enumerate an injected `IEnumerable<T>` only once: copy it into an array or `ImmutableArray` and build any indexes from that copy.** A lazy or non-repeatable sequence can yield different items each time, which leaves the list and its index disagreeing. *Check:* Look for constructors that enumerate an injected `IEnumerable<T>` more than once, for example with a collection expression and then a separate index build. <sub>Identity outcomes of #548</sub>
- **In production code, an implementation project references only `.Abstractions` packages and foundation packages, never another implementation project. It works with another capability through that capability's abstractions, resolved from DI.** References between implementations bring transitive dependencies, make the package boundary meaningless, and stop either implementation from being replaced on its own. *Check:* Inspect `ProjectReference` and `PackageReference` changes in implementation `.csproj` files for non-abstractions, non-foundation implementation projects. *Note:* Composition roots and hosts may reference concrete implementations. So may a documented layered framework reference, such as an Entity Framework slice that references the EF framework it plugs into. <sub>Identity ADR-1500; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, register a stateless capability as a singleton and run a long-running loop as a `BackgroundService` registered with `AddHostedService<T>`. Keep DI wiring in the project's registration class, following the repository's naming for it, and out of the types that do the work.** Worker types then stay constructor-injectable and testable, and a host replaces a default in one place. *Check:* Look for stateless services registered scoped or transient, loops started outside a hosted service, and working types that register themselves or resolve services from a provider. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, prefer an instance service behind an interface, registered as a singleton, to a `static` utility class. Keep `static` for pure functions, constants, extension entry points and immutable thread-safe shared instances such as a cached `JsonSerializerOptions`, and never use mutable static or ambient state.** Static utilities that have dependencies can't be substituted in tests, and mutable static state leaks between callers. *Check:* Look for new static classes that hold dependencies, do I/O or keep mutable static fields that collaborators depend on. *Note:* Don't report a static helper that is a pure function of its arguments, builds on sibling static helpers, and gets side-effecting dependencies such as a logger from its caller, for example through a delegate. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #835</sub>
- **When two registration methods register the same shared services, put those `TryAdd*` registrations in one private helper that both methods call.** Duplicated registration lists drift apart. *Check:* Look for repeated blocks of `TryAddSingleton`, `TryAddScoped` or `TryAddTransient` for the same services in sibling registration methods. *Note:* Don't report a `TryAdd*` registration as unused or duplicate when a service registered by the same method depends on it through its constructor and every duplicate is a `TryAdd*` of the same implementation. It lets the method work on its own. <sub>Identity outcomes of #629; Identity outcomes of #599</sub>
- **Keep `Program.cs` a flat list of `AddX`, `UseX` and `MapX` calls. Move conditionals, loops, policy builders, `new`, constants and configuration reads into an extension in the owning project, leaving only inputs specific to the host: the database provider and connection string, production secrets, and Kestrel HTTPS defaults.** Composition stays readable and features stay turnkey. *Check:* Look for logic, literals or configuration reads added to `Program.cs`. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Remove constructor-injected dependencies that the class stores but never reads.** A dead dependency makes readers check it for nothing and makes DI resolve a service for nothing. *Check:* Look for constructor parameters or properties, such as a `TimeProvider` carried over from copied code, that no member of the class reads. *Note:* A parameter that the repository's conventions require, such as a `CancellationToken` on every async method, isn't dead code. <sub>Identity outcomes of #555</sub>
- **Don't report an object that both the DI container and another owner dispose as a defect when both disposal paths are idempotent and the second owner is needed for instances that never pass through the container.** Idempotent disposal can't throw or release resources twice, and the extra owner disposes instances the container never created. *Check:* Before reporting, read the `Dispose`/`DisposeAsync` implementations for a guard such as `IsDisposed`, and check whether some instances bypass the container's factory. <sub>Identity outcomes of #709</sub>
- **In test projects, name every `IServiceCollection` local, parameter and lambda parameter `serviceCollection`. An `IServiceProvider` keeps its own name.** A service collection is then named the same way as in production code. *Check:* Look for `IServiceCollection` variables or lambda parameters named `services`, `s`, `collection` or anything else. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp-testing.instructions.md</sub>
